summary:
Recommendation: switch to ensure_vertical_shell_thickness = partial in the Etapa C test variant, and keep enabled in production until one test print passes inspection. Overall risk is medium-low. It is the largest time lever of the three candidates, at about -3.5 to -6 min per piece.

**What the code does (Bambu Studio 02.08.02.60, PrintObject::discover_vertical_shells)**
- Partial and enabled differ in one thing: whether `combine_holes(cache.holes)` runs over the 6 layers above and the 3 layers below.
- Both modes keep the top and bottom shells. Top surfaces are projected 6 layers down (5 from the layer count, plus 1 because top_shell_thickness is 1.0 mm and 6 x 0.16 = 0.96 mm). Bottom surfaces are projected 3 layers up.
- Only enabled adds "internal area minus the intersection of the infill areas of the neighbouring layers". On slopes this is a solid ribbon right behind the 2 walls: about 6 x step wide under upward-facing slopes and 3 x step under overhangs (step = how far the outline moves per layer).
- With "Detect narrow internal solid infill" on (detect_narrow_internal_solid_infill = 1), Fill.cpp relabels any narrow solid area (under 6 mm wide) that touches sparse infill on the layer below. The G-code then calls it "Floating vertical shell" and prints it with the concentric Arachne pattern. So the "Floating vertical shell" in the G-code is essentially these slope ribbons.
- Correction to the brief: detect_floating_vertical_shell does not create that role. It only marks segments that hang over sparse infill so they print at bridge speed, and here that marking applies to only 0.03 m of line.
- Disabled is a different algorithm (the older horizontal-shell pass). It was not evaluated.

**This part (G-code measurements plus a validated raster emulation of the mesh)**
- Floating vertical shell sits in Z 4–20 (inside of the ring hole, lower half, and the underside) and Z 28–52 (upper outer slopes and bird body). There is none between Z 19.7 and 26.3.
- Internal solid infill is the bottom shell at Z 0–4 and small solid areas at Z 48–64 (the heads), which come from minimum_sparse_infill_area = 15.
- The emulation is a pixel-grid re-implementation of this algorithm run on the 3MF mesh. Run with enabled, it predicts 1124 mm³ of solid; the real G-code has 1035 mm³ (Floating vertical shell + Internal solid infill + Bridge), and it agrees band by band.
- For partial it predicts about 70–75% of that solid disappears, roughly 700–775 mm³ per piece:
  - Z 12–48 drops to almost nothing.
  - Z 4–12 keeps part, on the shallow floor of the hole.
  - The heads (Z 48–64) keep most of their solid.
  - Bottom and top shells are kept.

**Time per piece**
- About -3.6 min from extrusion alone, net of the sparse infill that replaces it.
- Up to about -6 min if the 2562 short travel starts that lead into Floating vertical shell also disappear (125 s of travel overhead today).
- Production at acceleration 6000 will save somewhat less.
- These bands are not held back by the minimum layer time, so single-piece orders also save the time.

**Speed and role**
- Floating vertical shell already prints at the 7.5 mm³/s flow cap (about 120 mm/s at 0.42 mm), the same as internal solid infill.
- Its cost comes from very short segments (median 0.22 mm).
- The replaced area becomes gyroid sparse infill with longer segments (median 1.1 mm), at the same flow cap.

**Risk**
- Pinholes and pillowing: not increased. Top shells are unchanged, the G-code has only 76 mm of Top surface, and only 33 mm² of the mesh is near-flat facing up.
- Gyroid showing through: the main risk. On upward slopes 40–75° from horizontal (about 1650 mm², 27% of the surface, mostly Z 32–48 and Z 8–24), the shell becomes the 2 walls only. Measured perpendicular to the surface that is about 0.55–0.8 mm, against about 1.1–1.3 mm today.
- Stated as an expectation, not a measurement: the mid-height band (Z 20–28) already prints as 2 walls plus gyroid, so if no infill pattern shows through there on the current prints, it is a good sign for the slopes.

Evidence files: the source is under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-BlendDeMagnesio/9a1dcd43-de9f-5228-9312-5f6da0bc1200/scratchpad/src, and my scripts and outputs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-BlendDeMagnesio/9a1dcd43-de9f-5228-9312-5f6da0bc1200/scratchpad/research_c/evst/ (sim_evst.py is the emulation; evst_sim.json and evst_sim2.json are its results; estimate.py and overhead.py do the time estimates).

Shared-folder note: research_c/classic.json and research_c/scripts/{scan,bands}.py are mine and harmless. research_c/arachne.json was rewritten by another agent after my first scan, so I moved my work into evst/.

claims.claim: The only difference between partial and enabled in discover_vertical_shells is whether the infill areas ('holes') of the neighbouring layers are intersected. Partial keeps only the projected top and bottom surfaces, plus solid areas that already exist.
claims.evidence: scratchpad/src/libslic3r_PrintObject.cpp:1943-1947 "if (region_config.ensure_vertical_shell_thickness.value != EnsureVerticalThicknessLevel::evtPartial) { combine_holes(cache.holes); } combine_shells(cache.top_surfaces);"; :1974-1978 same for bottom_surfaces; :1870 holes = "to_polygons(layer.regions()[region_id]->fill_expolygons)"; :2003 "polygons_append(shell, diff(polygonsInternal, holes));". In partial, holes is the layer's own infill area, which already contains all internal areas, so this diff is empty.

claims.claim: Window: a top surface forces solid infill in the 6 layers below it, so the top shell is 7 layers (1.12 mm) including the top layer. That is 5 layers from top_shell_layers=6 plus 1 more from top_shell_thickness=1.0, because 6 x 0.16 = 0.96 mm < 1.0 mm. A bottom surface forces solid in 3 layers above it (4 total; bottom_shell_thickness=0). Enabled uses this same window for the hole intersection, so its slope ribbons are about 6 x step wide under upward-facing slopes and 3 x step under overhangs.

claims.claim: The resulting shell is regularized. Strips narrower than about 0.26 mm are opened away (that is why near-vertical walls get no ribbon). The rest is grown by about 0.08 mm, and pieces smaller than 0.61 mm², or smaller than 3.24 mm² and enclosed by the layers above and below, are dropped. For partial on this part, this filter removes most of the narrow, fragmented top-projection strips.

claims.claim: Correction to the brief: the 'Floating vertical shell' role is created by detect_narrow_internal_solid_infill, not by detect_floating_vertical_shell. Fill.cpp relabels any internal solid area that is too narrow to survive a 3 mm inward offset and touches sparse infill on the layer below, and prints it with the FloatingConcentric (Arachne) pattern. detect_floating_vertical_shell only marks segments over sparse infill so they print at bridge speed. Both are 1 in the G-code. Because the slope ribbons are narrow and partly sit on sparse infill, this role is essentially the enabled-mode ribbons.
claims.evidence: libslic3r_Fill_Fill.cpp:19 "#define NARROW_INFILL_AREA_THRESHOLD 3"; :463 "if (layer.object()->config().detect_narrow_internal_solid_infill)"; :503-506 "surface_fills[i].params.pattern = ipFloatingConcentric; ... extrusion_role = erFloatingVerticalShell"; libslic3r_Fill_FillFloatingConcentric.cpp:702 "detect_floating_line(..., !print_object_config->detect_floating_vertical_shell.value || is_self_intersect)"; G-code:77-78 "; detect_floating_vertical_shell = 1" / "; detect_narrow_internal_solid_infill = 1"

claims.claim: Speed: Floating vertical shell uses vertical_shell_speed (80% of internal_solid_infill_speed 200 = 160 mm/s), or bridge speed (50 mm/s here) for segments marked as floating. In practice both it and internal solid infill hit the 7.5 mm³/s flow cap, about 121 mm/s at 0.42 mm wide. Measured: Floating vertical shell runs at 70–140 mm/s with variable widths of 0.35–0.61 mm, and only 0.03 m prints at 50 mm/s or less. It is slow because its segments are tiny: 33,724 segments, median 0.216 mm, 84% of its length in segments under 1 mm. That gives 697 mm³ in 255 s, about 2.7 mm³/s, or 36% of the cap. Sparse infill segments have a median of 1.1 mm.

recommendation:
Switch to partial now in the Etapa C test variant. The risk is medium-low, and the change can be undone. Keep production on enabled until a test piece passes the inspection below.

Edit: in Metadata/project_settings.config (process), change "ensure_vertical_shell_thickness": "enabled" to "ensure_vertical_shell_thickness": "partial". The original 3MF has "enabled" at line 158 of that file. With the project tool: python3 -I gerar_variante_3mf.py ORIGINAL.3mf OUT.3mf ... --processo ensure_vertical_shell_thickness=partial. The tool also adds the key to different_settings_to_system[0], so Bambu Studio does not reset it.

Leave these unchanged, because they are what keeps top/bottom shell protection and the small solid areas in the heads: detect_narrow_internal_solid_infill=1, detect_floating_vertical_shell=1, vertical_shell_speed=80%, top_shell_layers=6, top_shell_thickness=1, bottom_shell_layers=4, wall_loops=2, minimum_sparse_infill_area=15.

Why for this part:
- About 70-75% of all solid infill (about 700-775 mm³ per piece) is slope ribbons. They exist only because enabled intersects the infill areas of the neighbouring layers.
- They print very inefficiently: about 2.7 mm³/s, plus 2562 short travels.
- Partial keeps everything that guards against pinholes and pillowing: the top shell under every top strip, the 4-layer bottom shell, and the small solid areas in the heads.
- The only loss is the extra 0.4-0.6 mm of solid backing behind the 2 walls on 40-75° upward slopes. That leaves those slopes with the same walls-plus-gyroid structure that the near-vertical mid band (Z 20-28) already has.

Test order:
- Do not stack this with sparse_infill_density 15% -> 12% or 10%, or with infill_combination=1, in the same first test.
- Both act on exactly the same zones: gyroid touching the walls on the slopes, with a wider pitch or thicker combined lines.
- Test partial at 15% gyroid first, or at least on a separate plate, so that any show-through can be traced to its cause.

If show-through appears on the upper slopes (Z 32-52) or inside the ring, go back to enabled. Do not compensate with a third wall, which would cost more time than partial saves.
expected_time_effect:
Expected direction: shorter, about -3.5 to -6 min per piece; central estimate about -4.5 min, or about -6-7% of the roughly 1h04-1h08 per piece in 4-up production.

How the estimate is built, from the 1-piece Arachne G-code:
- About 287 s of Floating vertical shell and internal solid infill extrusion goes away (about 222 s of it Floating vertical shell).
- About 60 s of extra sparse infill replaces it.
- Net about -227 s (-3.8 min) from extrusion alone.
- Removing the short travels and retractions in front of the Floating vertical shell starts could add about -100 to -130 s.

The removed solid sits in bands that are not held back by the 8 s minimum layer time, so single-piece orders save as well. In 4-up production at acceleration 6000, Floating vertical shell is already a bit faster per mm³, so the extrusion part of the saving shrinks by perhaps 10-15%.

Only slicing can confirm:
- how much solid the real area filter leaves (the simulation brackets it at 260-305 mm³);
- the real drop in travels and retractions;
- the exact replacement sparse volume;
- how the minimum-layer-time slowdown behaves at Z 52-64 for single-piece prints.
visual_risks: Gyroid showing through, or telegraphing as a faint pattern on the walls (15% gyroid, line pitch about 3 mm), on upward slopes 40-75° from horizontal. That is about 1650 mm², 27% of the surface: mostly the ring shoulders and bird body at Z 32-52, and the inside of the hole's lower half at Z 8-24. The shell there becomes 2 walls only, about 0.53-0.79 mm thick perpendicular to the surface, against about 1.1-1.3 mm with enabled. Silk shine shows small surface waves easily.

On 40-50° slopes, each layer's inner wall overhangs sparse infill by up to about 0.19 mm (about 40% of its 0.45 mm width). The inner wall may droop slightly between gyroid lines. The outer wall stays supported because the per-layer step is under 0.42 mm, so any visible effect should be weak.

Head tops at Z 56-64 (beak, snake head): partial keeps the small solid areas (minimum_sparse_infill_area 15) and the top projections, but drops about 50 mm³ of slope ribbon. Check fine detail and shine there.

Combining with the other Etapa C candidates makes it worse. Lower density widens the gyroid pitch to 3.75-4.5 mm, and infill_combination puts 0.32 mm-thick sparse lines against the same slope walls. Do not judge all three on one print.

Pinholes and pillowing: no added risk expected. Top shells (6 extra layers under any top strip) are unchanged, the part has only 33 mm² of near-flat upward surface, and the G-code has 76 mm of Top surface.
Overhang sides (underside on the tree supports at Z 0-8, ceiling of the hole at Z 28-36): ribbons removed, but appearance there is set by the walls and supports. Low risk.
Shell strength: thinner shells on the slopes. Acceptable for a decorative piece, but press-check the test piece.
